name: Foundations of Pre-Ophrasian Grammar and Script
author: Coll.
body: It has been well established that the wound of the Ophrasian War will not close in our lifetimes, yet it is our duty as scholars to document it and the world before it shattered. This collection is meant to be the reference on pre-Ophrasian linguistics, covering matters of syntax, semantics, phonology and lexicography of various languages now gone. The last part of this volume deals with the question of dialectal variation: some of these found(again) languages might actually be related even if they don't share isoglosses. While some call the proof inconsistent or far-fetched, both viewpoints are explored here.

name: Runebridge Companion: Occult Lore
author: Clemont Tarresh
body: This comprehensive volume, sanctioned by the Runebridge Oversight Committee, serves as the definitive academic survey of "extra-Ethyrian" phenomena within the Boundless Vale. While Ethyria—the interconnected threads of reality born from the fallen goddess Mystara—remains the primary medium for modern spellcraft, this Companion delves into the "liminal spaces" that exist beyond traditional arcane schools, but focuses mostly on the history and beliefs that surround these practices of what the laymen call "magick".

name: The Sleeper's Oath
author: Blythe Olinsher &  Ellia Runefoot
body:
Written during the Doleris era, The Sleeper’s Oath is a cosmological treatise on the Dreamlands, which the text refers to exclusively as the Saoghal. Rather than framing the dreamscape as a separate or parallel plane, the author posits a suffocating metaphysics: reality is composed of superimposed layers occupying the exact same physical coordinates. Material existence, the Saoghal, and deeper planar strata exist simultaneously beneath, above, and directly within the identical space.

The core of the treatise explores the hypothesis of something that exists through and beyond the Saoghal—a singular, terrifying presence or state of being that pierces all layers at once. As the work progresses, the author’s academic composure collapses into obsession. The phrase "through and beyond" begins as a technical descriptor for dimensional overlap, but gradually infects the entire work, interrupting formal proofs and recurring like an inescapable mental echo. To study its contents is to invite a profound cognitive vertigo, stripping away the boundary between waking and dreaming until physical space feels perforated by infinite, concurrent realities.

name: Memory as Mechanism
author: Unknown
body:
This old tome is an impenetrable philosophical treatise that approaches consciousness through a lens of cold, arcane determinism. Rejecting the notion of the mind as an ethereal soul or fluid spirit, the text treats the psyche as an immense, interlocking apparatus — a delicate clockwork of cognitive gears, escapements, and conduits where every thought, emotion, and perception is merely the output of an underlying structural process. Because it views consciousness as an engineered system, the work argues that the self is fundamentally modular: every component of the mind can be measured, calibrated, forcibly reconfigured, or irrevocably broken.

The core of the text focuses on the mechanics of memory, presenting it not as passive recollection, but as physical architecture. The author outlines exhaustive— and deeply unsettling — theories on how sensory experiences are engraved into mental substrates, how recall operates as a mechanical retrieval cycle, and how those impressions can be altered. Through dense, esoteric jargon and cryptic axiomatic proofs, the work details methods for splicing synthetic recollections into existing cognitive frameworks, shearing away specific memories without destabilizing the whole, or deliberately introducing stress fractures that cause a subject’s identity to suffer catastrophic systemic failure. For those who can parse its arcane syntax, the book reads less like traditional philosophy and more like a user’s manual for dissecting the sentient psyche.

name: Notes on the Everlasting
author: E. Gridgepot
body: This book explores the various interpretations of the Everlasting across different cultures and religions, as well as its potential influence on the events leading up to and following the schism of the Church of Arawan.

name: The Last Day
author: The Blind Seer
body: "When the first tide forgets the shore and the Four Pillars stand as one, the Great Anchor shall slip its chain. No ship shall rot in port, for the horizon has teeth to pull the bold into the skyless deep. They go not to the Shun Lands, but to the land that builds for no man; a sacrifice made to the silent reach where the map ends and the unobserved world begins."

name: The sultry deck-hand and the Sirens
author: Meleas Findregor
body:
The melodrama follows Jack "Bronze-Chested" Merriweather, an impossibly handsome sailor aboard the privateer brig Sea Nymph, whose linen shirts suffer an inexplicable tendency to rip open whenever a brisk ocean gale catches the rigging. When the vessel drifts into the cursed mists of the Serpent's Gulf, the crew scrambles to stuff beeswax into their ears against the lethal allure of the reefs. Jack, however, catches the eye of Sorsha—a haughty, silver-scaled siren sovereign who finds herself entirely unprepared for a mortal whose smoldering gaze rivals the fury of an arcane tempest.

What begins as a battle of wits and wills over the ship's fate quickly spirals into breathless moonlit confrontations, stolen embraces against the capstan, and dramatic declarations of passion whispered over the crash of breaking surf. Jack must ultimately decide whether to heed the strict code of the privateer brotherhood or surrender to the treacherous, intoxicating pull of the deep.

name: Meditations on the way of the lizard
author: Master Sshev
body:
Meditation on the Way of the Lizard is an obscure ascetic treatise documenting an all-but-extinct monastic discipline native to arid crags and subterranean ruins.

Penned by the hermit-ascetic Master Sshev of the Sunken Terraces, the text fundamentally rejects the fluid momentum of water styles and the fierce exertion of dragon disciplines, advocating instead for the profound power of absolute inertia. Sshev argues that ki is not summoned through relentless motion, but cultivated in motionless basking—absorbing the ambient heat and pressure of the world until mind and muscle enter a state of preserved suspended stillness. The treatise is structured around four core contemplative disciplines: Unblinking Perception (cultivating peripheral awareness while maintaining utter physical stillness), The Shed Tail (the philosophical and martial willingness to sacrifice superficial ego or flesh to preserve the vital core), The Clinging Palm (mastery of surface friction and vertical mobility), and The Sudden Tongue (unleashing explosive, lethal strikes without windup or telegraphing).

While orthodox monastic orders often criticized the Way of the Lizard as callous and cold-blooded—pointing to Sshev’s insistence that a master should let kingdoms burn around them if moving would break their inner equilibrium—the work is quietly revered by martial historians and assassins alike. Surviving copies are heavily annotated in the margins by centuries of curious initiates, all seeking Sshev’s lost methods for moving from complete rest to blinding lethality in the space of a single heartbeat.
